claim: RNA granules are ubiquitous cytoplasmic organelles that contain RNA and RNA-binding proteins.
source: RNA granules are ubiquitous cytoplasmic organelles that contain RNA and RNA-binding proteins (Kedersha et al., 2013; Buchan, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kedersha et al., 2013 and Buchan, 2014

claim: RNA granules include germ granules in germ cells, neuronal granules in neurons, and stress granules and P bodies in somatic cells.
source: Several types of RNA granules have been described, including germ granules in germ cells, neuronal granules in neurons, and stress granules and P bodies in somatic cells.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about RNA granule types

claim: RNA granule functions include mRNA transport and storage and the regulation of mRNA degradation and translation.
source: Their functions include mRNA transport and storage and the regulation of mRNA degradation and translation.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about RNA granule functions

claim: RNA granules are not bound by limiting membranes.
source: Unlike other organelles, RNA granules are not bound by limiting membranes and their internal components are in constant flux with the surrounding cytoplasm.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge distinguishing RNA granules from membrane-bound organelles

claim: RNA granule internal components are in constant flux with the surrounding cytoplasm.
source: Unlike other organelles, RNA granules are not bound by limiting membranes and their internal components are in constant flux with the surrounding cytoplasm.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about RNA granule dynamics

claim: RNA granules assemble and disassemble in response to developmental or environmental cues.
source: RNA granules assemble and disassemble in response to developmental or environmental cues (Kedersha et al., 2013; Buchan, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kedersha et al., 2013 and Buchan, 2014

claim: Live imaging studies in C. elegans zygotes have suggested that RNA granules behave like liquid droplets that undergo phase transitions.
source: Live imaging studies in Caenorhabditis elegans zygotes have suggested that RNA granules behave like liquid droplets that undergo phase transitions (Brangwynne et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brangwynne et al., 2009

claim: Granule components exist in a condensed liquid or gel-like phase in the granule and a dispersed phase in the cytoplasm.
source: Granule components exist in a condensed liquid or gel-like phase in the granule and a dispersed phase in the cytoplasm (Weber and Brangwynne, 2012; Toretsky and Wright, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Weber and Brangwynne, 2012 and Toretsky and Wright, 2014

claim: Proteins that contain weak, multivalent protein-binding domains undergo liquid–liquid demixing in concentrated solutions to form micron-sized droplets.
source: For example, proteins that contain weak, multivalent protein-binding domains undergo liquid–liquid demixing in concentrated solutions to form micron-sized droplets (Li et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2012

claim: RNA-binding proteins that contain low sequence-complexity domains assemble into ordered fibers that coalesce into hydrogels when maintained at low temperature.
source: Similarly, RNA-binding proteins that contain low sequence-complexity domains assemble into ordered fibers that coalesce into hydrogels when maintained at low temperature (Frey et al., 2006; Kato et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Frey et al., 2006 and Kato et al., 2012

claim: The kinase DYRK3 has been implicated in the regulation of stress granule dissolution and condensation.
source: recently the kinase DYRK3 has been implicated in the regulation of stress granule dissolution and condensation (Wippich et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wippich et al., 2013

claim: This study identifies the substrates of the C. elegans DYRK3 homolog MBK-2.
source: In the present study, we identify the substrates of the C. elegans DYRK3 homolog MBK-2 and demonstrate that phosphorylation and dephosphorylation of these substrates drive the dissolution and condensation of P granules in embryos.
evidence: Stated as a primary finding of the study

claim: Phosphorylation and dephosphorylation of MBK-2 substrates drive the dissolution and condensation of P granules in embryos.
source: In the present study, we identify the substrates of the C. elegans DYRK3 homolog MBK-2 and demonstrate that phosphorylation and dephosphorylation of these substrates drive the dissolution and condensation of P granules in embryos.
evidence: Stated as a primary finding of the study

claim: P granules are the germ granules of C. elegans.
source: P granules are the germ granules of C. elegans (Strome and Wood, 1982; Updike and Strome, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Strome and Wood, 1982 and Updike and Strome, 2010

claim: P granules are perinuclear during most of the germline development.
source: P granules are perinuclear during most of the germline development.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about P granule localization

claim: During the oocyte-to-embryo transition, P granules detach from nuclei and disperse in the cytoplasm for asymmetric segregation to the nascent embryonic germline.
source: During the oocyte-to-embryo transition, P granules detach from nuclei and disperse in the cytoplasm for asymmetric segregation to the nascent embryonic germline.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about P granule dynamics during development

claim: Preferential dissolution of P granules in the anterior and condensation in the posterior of the zygote cause the granules to accumulate in the cytoplasm destined for the germline blastomere P1.
source: Preferential dissolution of the granules in the anterior and condensation in the posterior of the zygote cause the granules to accumulate in the cytoplasm destined for the germline blastomere P1 (Figure 1) (Brangwynne et al., 2009; Gallo et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brangwynne et al., 2009 and Gallo et al., 2010, and shown in Figure 1

claim: P granules segregate asymmetrically for three more divisions until the P granules are uniquely concentrated in the germline founder cell P4.
source: P granules segregate asymmetrically for three more divisions until the P granules are uniquely concentrated in the germline founder cell P4 (Strome and Wood, 1983).
evidence: Supported by citation to Strome and Wood, 1983

claim: The RGG domain proteins PGL-1 and PGL-3 and the Vasa-related helicases GLH-1, 2, 3, and 4 form the core components of P granules.
source: Two groups of RNA-binding proteins form the core components of P granules: the RGG domain proteins PGL-1 and PGL-3 and the Vasa-related helicases GLH-1, 2, 3, and 4 (Updike and Strome, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Updike and Strome, 2010

claim: A self-association domain in the PGL family is essential for granule nucleation.
source: A self-association domain in the PGL family is essential for granule nucleation (Hanazawa et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hanazawa et al., 2011

claim: FG repeats in GLH-1 are required for P granules to associate with nuclei.
source: FG repeats in GLH-1 are required for P granules to associate with nuclei (Updike et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Updike et al., 2011

claim: MBK-2 is the C. elegans DYRK3 homolog.
source: In previous studies, we identified two potential regulators of P granule dynamics: MBK-2, the C. elegans DYRK3 homolog (Aranda et al., 2011; Wippich et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Aranda et al., 2011 and Wippich et al., 2013

claim: PPTR-1 is a regulatory subunit of the heterotrimeric phosphatase PP2A.
source: PPTR-1, a regulatory subunit of the heterotrimeric phosphatase PP2A (Padmanabhan et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Padmanabhan et al., 2009

claim: Loss of mbk-2 and pptr-1 has opposite effects on P granule dynamics.
source: Loss of mbk-2 and pptr-1 has opposite effects on P granule dynamics.
evidence: Stated as a finding from previous studies

claim: All P granules remain condensed in mbk-2 zygotes.
source: All P granules remain condensed in mbk-2 zygotes and all P granules disperse in pptr-1 zygotes (Pellettieri et al., 2003; Quintin et al., 2003; Gallo et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pellettieri et al., 2003, Quintin et al., 2003, and Gallo et al., 2010

claim: All P granules disperse in pptr-1 zygotes.
source: All P granules remain condensed in mbk-2 zygotes and all P granules disperse in pptr-1 zygotes (Pellettieri et al., 2003; Quintin et al., 2003; Gallo et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pellettieri et al., 2003, Quintin et al., 2003, and Gallo et al., 2010

claim: Shortly after ovulation, P granules that were present in the oocyte cytoplasm (oocyte granules) disassemble and new granules (zygote granules) form throughout the cytoplasm as the maternal pronucleus completes the second meiotic division.
source: Shortly after ovulation, P granules that were present in the oocyte cytoplasm (oocyte granules) disassemble and new granules (zygote granules) form throughout the cytoplasm as the maternal pronucleus completes the second meiotic division (Video 1, Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Video 1, Figure 1A, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: After meiosis, as the zygote becomes polarized along the anterior/posterior axis, granules in the anterior cytoplasm are quickly disassembled and granules in the posterior cytoplasm continue to grow and fuse to form large (≥1 micron) granules.
source: After meiosis, as the zygote becomes polarized along the anterior/posterior axis, granules in the anterior cytoplasm are quickly disassembled and granules in the posterior cytoplasm continue to grow and fuse to form large (≥1 micron) granules (Figure 1, Video 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1 and Video 2

claim: In zygotes derived from mothers lacking mbk-2, oocyte granule disassembly and zygote granule assembly proceeded as in wild-type during meiosis.
source: We found that in zygotes derived from mothers lacking mbk-2 (hereafter referred to as mbk-2 zygotes), oocyte granule disassembly and zygote granule assembly proceeded as in wild-type during meiosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: In mbk-2 zygotes, the zygote granules failed to disassemble in the anterior cytoplasm during zygote polarization.
source: The zygote granules, however, failed to disassemble in the anterior cytoplasm during zygote polarization (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B

claim: In pptr-1 mutant zygotes, disassembly of oocyte granules and assembly of zygotic granules proceeded normally during meiosis.
source: In pptr-1 mutant zygotes, disassembly of oocyte granules and assembly of zygotic granules proceeded normally during meiosis.
evidence: Stated as an observation from the study

claim: In pptr-1 mutant zygotes, after meiosis, granules in the posterior did not grow and all granules eventually disassembled by the onset of mitosis.
source: After meiosis, however, granules in the posterior did not grow (Figure 1B) and all granules eventually disassembled by the onset of mitosis, as previously reported (Gallo et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B and citation to Gallo et al., 2010

claim: PPTR-1 is 58% identical at the amino acid level to PPTR-2, another predicted B′/B56 regulatory subunit of PP2A.
source: PPTR-1 is 58% identical at the amino acid level to PPTR-2, another predicted B′/B56 regulatory subunit of PP2A (WormBase; [Harris et al., 2014]).
evidence: Supported by citation to WormBase and Harris et al., 2014

claim: In pptr-1 pptr-2, zygote granule assembly during meiosis was less robust and disassembly began even earlier during pronuclear migration.
source: In pptr-1 pptr-2, zygote granule assembly during meiosis was less robust and disassembly began even earlier during pronuclear migration (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: pptr-2 single mutants appeared as wild-type.
source: pptr-2 single mutants appeared as wild-type (data not shown).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the study

claim: pptr-1 and pptr-2 contribute redundantly to the assembly/stabilization of P granules in zygotes.
source: We conclude that pptr-1 and pptr-2 contribute redundantly to the assembly/stabilization of P granules in zygotes.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental observations

claim: When mbk-2 is depleted in pptr-1 pptr-2, new P granules assembled in the zygote and remained stable through the first division.
source: Intriguingly, when we depleted mbk-2 in pptr-1 pptr-2, we observed the same phenotype as in mbk-2: new P granules assembled in the zygote and remained stable through the first division (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B

claim: mbk-2 is epistatic to pptr-1 pptr-2.
source: mbk-2 therefore is epistatic to pptr-1 pptr-2, as might be expected in a 'no phosphorylation' scenario.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from genetic interaction experiments

claim: MBK-2 and PP2APPTR−1/2 work in opposition to promote P granule disassembly (MBK-2) and re-assembly (PP2APPTR−1/2).
source: These observations suggest that MBK-2 and PP2APPTR−1/2 work in opposition to promote P granule disassembly (MBK-2) and re-assembly (PP2APPTR−1/2).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental observations

claim: From 1.2 × 107 transformants in a yeast two-hybrid screen, approximately 4500 positive colonies were obtained.
source: From 1.2 × 107 transformants, we obtained ∼4500 positive colonies.
evidence: Stated as a result from the yeast two-hybrid screen

claim: Three genes were identified from the yeast two-hybrid screen that showed defects in P granule distribution or suppression of the pptr-1 phenotype: meg-1, F52D2.4, and C36C9.1.
source: We tested each gene by RNAi (1) for defects in P granule distribution in wild-type embryos, or (2) for suppression of the pptr-1 hyper-granule disassembly phenotype and identified three genes: meg-1, F52D2.4, and C36C9.1 (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Stated as a result from the screen

claim: meg-1 (and its paralog meg-2) was identified previously as a P granule component specific to early embryos.
source: meg-1 (and its paralog meg-2) was identified previously as a P granule component specific to early embryos (Leacock and Reinke, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Leacock and Reinke, 2008

claim: F52D2.4 was identified previously in a yeast two-hybrid screen as a gex-3 interactor and named gei-12.
source: F52D2.4 was identified previously in a yeast two-hybrid screen as a gex-3 interactor and named gei-12 (Tsuboi et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsuboi et al., 2002

claim: F52D2.4 has been renamed meg-3 based on the findings of this study.
source: Based on our findings (see below), we have renamed this gene meg-3.
evidence: Stated as a nomenclature decision based on study findings

claim: C36C9.1 is 71% identical to F52D2.4/meg-3 at the amino acid level.
source: C36C9.1 is 71% identical to F52D2.4/meg-3 at the amino acid level, and we have named it meg-4 (Figure 2).
evidence: Stated as a sequence analysis result shown in Figure 2

claim: meg-3 and meg-4 were identified previously as pptr-2 interactors in a genome-wide yeast two-hybrid screen.
source: meg-3 and meg-4 were identified previously as pptr-2 interactors in a genome-wide yeast two-hybrid screen (Simonis et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Simonis et al., 2009

claim: All four meg genes are X-linked and code for 70–95.8 kDa proteins that contain 11.8–14.3% serine and 7.2–9.6% asparagine residues and >60% residues predicted to be in disordered regions.
source: All four meg genes are X-linked and code for 70–95.8 kDa proteins that contain 11.8–14.3% serine and 7.2–9.6% asparagine residues and >60% residues predicted to be in disordered regions (Figure 2).
evidence: Stated as a sequence analysis result shown in Figure 2

claim: meg-1/2 are not homologous to meg-3/4.
source: meg-1/2, however, are not homologous to meg-3/4 (WormBase; [Harris et al., 2014]).
evidence: Supported by citation to WormBase and Harris et al., 2014

claim: MEG-1, MEG-3, and MEG-4 bind directly to PPTR-1 and/or PPTR-2.
source: To test that the MEG-1, MEG-3, and MEG-4 proteins interact directly with PPTR-1 and PPTR-2, we performed GST pull down assays (Figure 3A). We found that all three bound to PPTR-1 and/or PPTR-2 but not to maltose-binding protein (MBP) or to PAA-1, the scaffolding subunit of PP2A.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A

claim: MEG-1, MEG-3, and MEG-4 do not bind to maltose-binding protein (MBP) or to PAA-1, the scaffolding subunit of PP2A.
source: We found that all three bound to PPTR-1 and/or PPTR-2 but not to maltose-binding protein (MBP) or to PAA-1, the scaffolding subunit of PP2A.
evidence: Stated as a result from GST pull down assays

claim: MEG-1, MEG-3, and MEG-4 interact with the P granule component PGL-1.
source: MEG-1, MEG-3, and MEG-4 also interacted with the P granule component PGL-1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Recombinant MBK-2 can phosphorylate MBP::MEG-1 and MBP::MEG-3, but not MBP alone.
source: MBK-2 could phosphorylate MBP::MEG-1 and MBP::MEG-3, but not MBP alone (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3B from in vitro kinase assays

claim: Phosphorylation of MEG-3 was reduced but not eliminated in the MEG-3(T541A S582A T605A) mutant.
source: Phosphorylation was reduced but not eliminated in the alanine mutants (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3B from in vitro kinase assays

claim: Phosphorylation of MEG-1 was reduced but not eliminated in the MEG-1(S574A) mutant.
source: Phosphorylation was reduced but not eliminated in the alanine mutants (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3B from in vitro kinase assays

claim: Recombinant MBK-2 phosphorylates MEG-1 and MEG-3 on consensus sites in vitro, as well as other sites that remain to be determined.
source: We conclude that recombinant MBK-2 phosphorylates MEG-1 and MEG-3 on consensus sites in vitro, as well as other sites that remain to be determined.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from in vitro kinase assay results

claim: Treatment with alkaline phosphatase eliminated the higher molecular weight species of GFP::MEG-1 and GFP::MEG-3 and increased the intensity of the lower species (unphosphorylated isoform).
source: Treatment with alkaline phosphatase eliminated the higher molecular weight species and increased the intensity of the lower species (unphosphorylated isoform, Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The relative abundance of the unphosphorylated isoform of MEG-1 and MEG-3 increased in lysates depleted of mbk-2.
source: The relative abundance of the unphosphorylated isoform increased in lysates depleted of mbk-2 and decreased in lysates depleted of pptr-1 (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C and 3D

claim: The relative abundance of the unphosphorylated isoform of MEG-1 and MEG-3 decreased in lysates depleted of pptr-1.
source: The relative abundance of the unphosphorylated isoform increased in lysates depleted of mbk-2 and decreased in lysates depleted of pptr-1 (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C and 3D

claim: MEG-1 and MEG-3 are phosphoproteins in vivo.
source: We conclude that MEG-1 and MEG-3 are phosphoproteins in vivo and that MBK-2 and PPTR-1 promote and antagonize, respectively, their phosphorylation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from Phos-tag gel experiments

claim: MBK-2 and PPTR-1 promote and antagonize, respectively, the phosphorylation of MEG-1 and MEG-3.
source: We conclude that MEG-1 and MEG-3 are phosphoproteins in vivo and that MBK-2 and PPTR-1 promote and antagonize, respectively, their phosphorylation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from Phos-tag gel experiments

claim: meg-3(tm4259) is an out-of-frame, 623-nucleotide deletion that creates a frameshift at amino acid 165 followed by premature stop at amino acid 170 and therefore is a likely null.
source: tm4259 is an out-of-frame, 623-nucleotide deletion that creates a frameshift at amino acid 165 followed by premature stop at amino acid 170 and therefore is a likely null (Figure 2).
evidence: Stated as a characterization of the allele shown in Figure 2

claim: meg-4(ax2026) is a 7 bp deletion which causes a frameshift at amino acid 13, followed by a premature stop at amino acid 48.
source: meg-4(ax2026) is a 7 bp deletion which causes a frameshift at amino acid 13, followed by a premature stop at amino acid 48 (Figure 2).
evidence: Stated as a characterization of the allele shown in Figure 2

claim: meg-4(ax2081) is a 3.2 kb deletion that removes 733 bases upstream of the meg-4 ATG and 2565 bases of the meg-4 coding sequence.
source: meg-4(ax2081) is a 3.2 kb deletion that removes 733 bases upstream of the meg-4 ATG and 2565 bases of the meg-4 coding sequence (total length: 2589 bases).
evidence: Stated as a characterization of the allele

claim: Disassembly of oocyte granules was incomplete in meg-3 meg-4 zygotes, causing a few oocyte granules to persist through the first mitotic division.
source: First, we noticed that disassembly of oocyte granules was incomplete in meg-3 meg-4 zygotes (Video 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), causing a few oocyte granules to persist through the first mitotic division (arrows in Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Video 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Figure 4A

claim: During mitosis in meg-3 meg-4 zygotes, a few new granules appeared in the posterior cytoplasm, but these remained small (<1 micron) and most were not maintained during the division.
source: During mitosis, a few new granules appeared in the posterior cytoplasm (Figure 4A), but these remained small (<1 micron) and most were not maintained during the division (Video 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A and Video 2

claim: The total number of granules in meg-3 meg-4 zygotes in mitosis was approximately 11% that of wild-type.
source: As a result, the total number of granules (including oocyte granules) in meg-3 meg-4 zygotes in mitosis was ∼11% that of wild-type (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4B

claim: In the 2-cell stage of meg-3 meg-4 embryos, new small granules formed again transiently in P1, but these were fewer and smaller than in wild-type.
source: In the 2-cell stage, new small granules formed again transiently in P1, but again these were fewer and smaller than in wild-type (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A

claim: By the 28-cell stage in meg-3 meg-4 embryos, only a few scattered granules were observed throughout the embryo, with no detectable enrichment in the germline founder cell P4.
source: This pattern was repeated at each division such that by the 28-cell stage, only a few scattered granules were observed throughout the embryo, with no detectable enrichment in the germline founder cell P4 (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A

claim: meg-3 meg-4 zygotes showed similar levels of overall GFP:PGL-1 fluorescence compared to wild-type.
source: meg-3 meg-4 zygotes showed similar levels of overall GFP:PGL-1 fluorescence compared to wild-type and similar levels of PGL-3 by western blot analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5

claim: meg-3 meg-4 zygotes showed similar levels of PGL-3 by western blot analysis compared to wild-type.
source: meg-3 meg-4 zygotes showed similar levels of overall GFP:PGL-1 fluorescence compared to wild-type and similar levels of PGL-3 by western blot analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5

claim: The loss of meg-3 and meg-4 causes a dramatic reduction in the number of P granules but does not affect PGL-1 and PGL-3 levels significantly.
source: We conclude that the loss of meg-3 and meg-4 causes a dramatic reduction in the number of P granules but does not affect PGL-1 and PGL-3 levels significantly.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental observations

claim: In meg-3 single mutants, oocyte granule disassembly was delayed but was eventually completed before the first division.
source: In meg-3 zygotes, oocyte granule disassembly was delayed but was eventually completed before the first division (Video 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Video 3

claim: Zygote granule assembly was impaired in meg-3 zygotes, with a 30% reduction in the number of P granules compared to wild-type.
source: Zygote granule assembly was also impaired, but less than in meg-3 meg-4 zygotes: we observed a 30% reduction in the number of P granules in meg-3 zygotes compared to the 89% reduction for meg-3 meg-4 zygotes (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4B

claim: A slight reduction in P granule number was observed in meg-4 zygotes.
source: We also observed only a slight reduction in P granule number in meg-4 zygotes (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4B

claim: meg-3 and meg-4 contribute redundantly to the assembly of zygote granules, with meg-3 providing the greater contribution.
source: We conclude that meg-3 and meg-4 contribute redundantly to the assembly of zygote granules, with meg-3 providing the greater contribution.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental observations

claim: In meg-3 meg-4 zygotes, nos-2 RNA was distributed equally to P blastomeres and their somatic sisters.
source: In meg-3 meg-4 zygotes, we found that nos-2 RNA was distributed equally to P blastomeres and their somatic sisters, consistent with the lack of stable P granules.
evidence: Stated as an observation from the study

claim: In meg-3 meg-4 zygotes, nos-2 RNA was still quickly degraded in the somatic blastomeres after division as in wild-type.
source: nos-2 RNA, however, was still quickly degraded in the somatic blastomeres after division as in wild-type (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A

claim: Loss of meg-3 and meg-4 did not affect the formation of P bodies.
source: Loss of meg-3 and meg-4 also did not affect the formation of P bodies (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B

claim: Loss of meg-3 and meg-4 did not affect the distribution of asymmetric proteins that segregate independently of P granules (PIE-1 and MEX-5).
source: Loss of meg-3 and meg-4 also did not affect the formation of P bodies (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B) nor the distribution of asymmetric proteins that segregate independently of P granules (PIE-1 and MEX-5) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C

claim: By the L1 larval stage, low levels of perinuclear P granules became visible in the primordial germ cells of meg-3 meg-4 double mutants.
source: By the L1 larval stage, when new P granule components are synthesized in the PGCs (Kawasaki et al., 2004), low levels of perinuclear P granules became visible in the primordial germ cells of meg-3 meg-4 double mutants (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4D and citation to Kawasaki et al., 2004

claim: By the L4 larval stage, P granule levels were indistinguishable from wild-type in fertile meg-3 meg-4 mutants.
source: By the L4 larval stage, P granule levels were indistinguishable from wild-type in fertile meg-3 meg-4 mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D

claim: MEG-3 and MEG-4 are only required for P granule assembly in pre-gastrulation embryos and are not required for other soma/germline asymmetries, or for the assembly of P bodies or perinuclear P granules.
source: We conclude that MEG-3 and MEG-4 are only required for P granule assembly in pre-gastrulation embryos and are not required for other soma/germline asymmetries, or for the assembly of P bodies or perinuclear P granules.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental observations

claim: In 2-cell stage meg-1 mutants, P granules failed to disassemble in the anterior cytoplasm of the P1 blastomere.
source: In 2-cell stage meg-1 mutants, P granules failed to disassemble in the anterior cytoplasm of the P1 blastomere (Figure 4A), causing a few P granules to be inherited by the EMS blastomere (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A

claim: meg-2(RNAi) on meg-1 mutants enhanced the percent of P granule missegregation to somatic blastomeres.
source: meg-2(RNAi) on meg-1 mutants enhanced the percent of P granule missegregation to somatic blastomeres (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B), as reported previously (Leacock and Reinke, 2008).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B and citation to Leacock and Reinke, 2008

claim: meg-1 and meg-2 contribute only weakly to granule assembly and contribute primarily to granule disassembly.
source: We conclude that, unlike meg-3 and meg-4, meg-1 and meg-2 contribute only weakly to granule assembly and contribute primarily to granule disassembly.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental observations

claim: The P granule assembly defects observed in meg-3 and meg-3 meg-4 zygotes were not affected by the additional loss of meg-1 or meg-1 and meg-2.
source: We found that the P granule assembly defects observed in meg-3 and meg-3 meg-4 zygotes were not affected by the additional loss of meg-1 or meg-1 and meg-2 (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 3C

claim: meg-3 and meg-4 are the primary contributors to granule assembly in early embryos.
source: We conclude that meg-3 and meg-4 are the primary contributors to granule assembly in early embryos, and that none of the megs are required for the assembly of perinuclear granules in PGCs later in development.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental observations

claim: None of the megs are required for the assembly of perinuclear granules in PGCs later in development.
source: We conclude that meg-3 and meg-4 are the primary contributors to granule assembly in early embryos, and that none of the megs are required for the assembly of perinuclear granules in PGCs later in development.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental observations

claim: meg-1 meg-2 double mutants are 100% sterile.
source: meg-1 meg-2 double mutants are 100% sterile (Leacock and Reinke, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Leacock and Reinke, 2008

claim: 27% of meg-3 meg-4 mutants were sterile.
source: We found that 27% of meg-3 meg-4 mutants and 100% of meg-1 meg-3 meg-4 mutants were sterile (Figure 4C).

claim: Overall granule shape was dynamic, with none of the granules maintaining a perfectly spherical shape.

claim: Granules remained close to each other for several seconds before initiating fusion.

claim: Dephosphorylation of the MEGs by PP2APPTR−1/PPTR2 promotes the stabilizing function of the MEGs.

claim: The MEGs contribute redundantly to a second activity required for germline proliferation during larval development.

source: Consistent with that view, fertile meg mutants that do not assemble P granules in the germ plasm assemble perinuclear P granules de novo later in development.
evidence: Stated as an observation from the study

claim: De novo assembly of perinuclear germ granules is also observed in animals that do not inherit germ plasm and specify their primordial germ cells through inductive mechanisms later in development.
source: De novo assembly of perinuclear germ granules is also observed in animals that do not inherit germ plasm and specify their primordial germ cells through inductive mechanisms later in development (Voronina et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Voronina et al., 2011

claim: Asymmetric segregation of core P granule components is not essential to distinguish germline from soma in embryos.
source: Previously, our analyses of pptr-1 mutants led us to conclude that asymmetric segregation of core P granule components is not essential to distinguish germline from soma in embryos (Gallo et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gallo et al., 2010

claim: The essential activity of the germ plasm resides not in the assembly of P granules per se but in the MEG proteins that regulate granule assembly.
source: Our results here support this view and suggest that the essential activity of the germ plasm resides not in the assembly of P granules per se but in the MEG proteins that regulate granule assembly.
evidence: Stated as a primary conclusion of the study
